To a language model, berry is token nineteen seven seven two. Two doors down, at nineteen seven seven oh, sits teeth. And cherry? Way off at sixty thousand two twenty-five. By the numbers, berry's a lot more like teeth. Which is nonsense. IDs are just labels. So the first thing the model does is swap each ID for a vector, a list of a few thousand numbers. That list is the token's embedding, looked up in a table the model learned in training.

And lists of numbers have geometry. They can sit close together, or far apart. Here's the lesson's tiny version, with three numbers per word. Measure from cat. Kitten's nearest, then dog. Wolf's further out, and truck's way over there. Nobody wrote that down. Training pushes words that turn up in similar sentences toward similar vectors. So once a model's seen the cat sat on the mat, the dog sat on the mat is half handled already. One catch. We named these three dimensions so we could read them. Real ones have no names. Dimension eighteen forty-seven of a real model doesn't mean anything you could point to. The meaning's in the whole arrangement.

And embeddings on their own can't see order. Dog bites man, and man bites dog, are the same three vectors, shuffled. Add them up, and both sentences come out exactly the same.
